originalTitle: Warren Buffett’s 10-Year Rule for a 68-Year-Old With $650,000 in an IRA and $3,000 a Month in Social Security. Here’s the Monthly Income and the Tax Bill.
summary: Warren Buffett's 1996 test for owning a stock, applied to a 68-year-old with $650,000 in an IRA and $3,000 a month in Social Security: $300,000 goes into a Treasury ladder paying about 4.9%, $350,000 into an S&P 500 index fund, the income is $5,500 a month and the federal tax bill is about $2,400 a year.
content:
Warren Buffett has a ten-year test, and he put it in one sentence in his 1996 letter to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders: "If you aren’t willing to own a stock for ten years, don’t even think about owning it for ten minutes." In the same letter he told most investors that the best way to own stocks is "through an index fund that charges minimal fees."

He wrote that sentence about choosing a business to own. Turned around and applied to a retiree’s money, it reads this way: any dollar you will spend inside ten years is not ten-year money, and it does not belong in stocks. The limit of that reading is the price of safety: the dollars kept out of stocks lock in today’s Treasury yields and give up whatever stocks earn on them over the decade.

So here is the ten-year test applied to a common case, a scenario built for the arithmetic: a 68-year-old who retired in June, single, with $650,000 in a rollover IRA and $3,000 a month from Social Security, who wants $5,500 a month to live on. The questions are how much of the $650,000 can be in stocks, what the monthly income is, and what the IRS takes.

Social Security covers $3,000 of the $5,500. The IRA covers the other $2,500 a month, $30,000 a year, which is 4.6% of the account in year one.

Ten years of that is $300,000. By Buffett’s test, that money fails. You will spend it before ten years are up, so it should never see a stock. The other $350,000 passes the test. You will not touch it for a decade, so it goes into a very low-cost S&P 500 index fund, the kind Buffett has named for his own family’s money. The split comes out at 54% stocks and 46% Treasuries.

The $300,000 goes into a ladder of Treasury notes inside the IRA, one maturing each year for ten years. As of Wednesday the 2-year Treasury paid 4.86%, the 5-year 4.95% and the 10-year 5.10%, according to Treasury data. The 10-year first closed above 5% in September, a level it had not reached since July 2007.

Call the ladder’s blended yield about 4.9%. That is $14,700 of interest in year one, about $1,225 a month, and it stays inside the IRA untaxed until it is withdrawn. Each year one note matures and pays that year’s $30,000. The interest is the cushion: it is what pays for a raise when prices rise, and in a year when stocks fall it means the fund is never sold at the bottom.

Add it up and this retiree has $5,500 a month coming in, $66,000 a year, with $36,000 of it from Social Security and $30,000 from the IRA.

The portfolio earns a good share of that on its own. The ladder pays $14,700. The stock side buys about 505 shares of Vanguard’s S&P 500 ETF at Friday’s close of $693.38, and those shares paid $7.43 each in dividends over the past 12 months, a yield of 1.07%, so about $3,700 a year. Interest and dividends together come to $18,400, more than half the withdrawal, before a single share is sold.

The IRS decides how much of your Social Security is taxable by adding your other income to half your benefit. For this retiree that is $30,000 from the IRA plus half of $36,000, which is $48,000. That is above the $34,000 line for a single filer, so run the worksheet in IRS Publication 915 and $16,400 of the $36,000 benefit counts as income. The other $19,600 is tax free.

Total income for federal purposes is $30,000 plus $16,400, which is $46,400.

Now the deductions. For 2026 the standard deduction for a single filer is $16,100. Anyone 65 or older gets an extra $2,050. And the tax law passed in 2025 added a deduction of up to $6,000 for people 65 and older through 2028, which this retiree gets in full because income is under the $75,000 level where it starts to shrink. Those three add up to $24,150.

Taxable income is $46,400 minus $24,150, which is $22,250. The first $12,400 is taxed at 10%, which is $1,240, and the remaining $9,850 at 12%, which is $1,182. The federal bill is $2,422 for the year, call it $2,400. That is 3.7% of the $66,000 this retiree spends, and it leaves about $5,300 a month after federal tax. Most states do not tax Social Security at all.

Born in 1958, this retiree starts required withdrawals at 73, in 2031. That leaves five years in which the IRA can be moved into a Roth a slice at a time at low rates.

Filling the rest of the 12% bracket allows a conversion of $15,200 a year. The extra federal tax on it is $3,400, an effective rate of 22.2% on the converted dollars, because every dollar converted also pulls more Social Security into the taxable column, until 81% of the benefit is taxed. Five years of that moves $76,000 into a Roth, where it grows with no required withdrawals and comes out tax free. Even with the conversion, income stays $34,480 under the $109,000 line where Medicare’s Part B premium of $202.90 a month starts to carry a surcharge.

Assume the stock side earns 7% a year, well under the 15.2% the S&P 500 returned over the past ten years, the ladder keeps paying 4.9%, and the withdrawal rises 2.5% a year. By 73 the ladder has spent down to about $208,000, the fund has grown to about $491,000, and the IRA holds about $700,000.

The first required withdrawal on $700,000 is $700,000 divided by 26.5, the IRS divisor at 73, which is $26,400. By then the plan is already drawing $33,900 a year, so the required amount forces nothing extra out. The job at 73 is different: sell enough of the fund in a good year to put ten years of withdrawals back into the ladder.

The ten-year test is a bet that the stock side will have a decade to work. The last ten years would have turned $350,000 into about $1.44 million with dividends reinvested, by the S&P 500 fund’s record from November 2016 to this week. The worst ten calendar years in the same record, the end of 1999 to the end of 2009, lost about 10% with dividends reinvested, and would have left $316,000. The ladder is what lets you wait that out without selling.

chineseTitle: 沃伦·巴菲特对 68 岁的 IRA 账户有 65 万美元，社会保障每月有 3,000 美元的 10 年规则。这是月收入和税单。
chineseSummary: 沃伦·巴菲特 1996 年对拥有股票的测试，适用于一位 68 岁的人，IRA 中有 65 万美元，社会保障每月有 3,000 美元：30 万美元进入财政部阶梯，支付约 4.9%，35 万美元进入标准普尔 500 指数基金，每月收入为 5,500 美元，联邦税单约为每年 2,400 美元。
chineseContent:
沃伦·巴菲特有一个十年测试，他在 1996 年致伯克希尔·哈撒韦公司股东的信中用一句话概括了这一点：“如果你不愿意持有一只股票十年，那就别想拥有它十分钟。”在同一封信中，他告诉大多数投资者，拥有股票的最佳方式是“通过收取最低费用的指数基金”。

他写下了关于选择拥有一家企业的那句话。反过来，应用于退休人员的钱，它是这样写的：你在十年内花的任何美元都不是十年钱，它不属于股票。这种解读的极限是安全的价格：远离股票的美元锁定了今天的国债收益率，并放弃了过去十年股票从中赚取的任何收益。

因此，这里是适用于一个常见案例的十年测试，一个为算术而构建的场景：一名 68 岁的单身人士，于 6 月退休，个人退休账户 (IRA) 转存为 65 万美元，每月社会保障金为 3,000 美元，他希望每月有 5,500 美元的生活费。问题是 65 万美元中有多少可以投资股票、每月收入是多少以及国税局会收取什么。

社会保障涵盖 5,500 美元中的 3,000 美元。 IRA 每月支付另外 2,500 美元，每年 30,000 美元，占第一年账户的 4.6%。

十年就是 30 万美元。根据巴菲特的测试，这笔钱失败了。你会在十年到期之前花掉它，所以它永远不会看到股票。另外 350,000 美元通过了测试。你十年之内都不会碰它，所以它会被投入一只成本非常低的标准普尔 500 指数基金，巴菲特以自己家族的钱命名的那种基金。此次拆分后，股票占 54%，国债占 46%。

这 30 万美元进入 IRA 内的一系列国库券，每年到期一次，为期十年。根据财政部数据，截至周三，2年期国债利率为4.86%，5年期国债利率为4.95%，10年期国债利率为5.10%。 9 月份，10 年期国债首次收于 5% 以上，这是自 2007 年 7 月以来从未达到过的水平。

阶梯的混合收益率约为 4.9%。第一年的利息为 14,700 美元，每月约 1,225 美元，并且在提取之前一直保留在 IRA 中，不征税。每年一张票据到期并支付当年的 30,000 美元。利息是缓冲：当价格上涨时，利息是用来支付加息的费用，而在股票下跌的一年中，这意味着基金永远不会在底部出售。

加起来，这位退休人员每月收入 5,500 美元，每年收入 66,000 美元，其中 36,000 美元来自社会保障，30,000 美元来自 IRA。

该投资组合本身就获得了很大一部分收益。梯子支付 14,700 美元。股票方在周五收盘价为 693.38 美元时购买了约 505 股 Vanguard 标普 500 ETF 股票，这些股票在过去 12 个月中每股支付了 7.43 美元的股息，收益率为 1.07%，因此每年约为 3,700 美元。在出售一股之前，利息和股息合计达到 18,400 美元，超过一半的提款额。

美国国税局通过将您的其他收入加到您福利的一半来决定您的社会保障的应税金额。对于这位退休人员，IRA 提供 30,000 美元，加上 36,000 美元的一半，即 48,000 美元。这高于单个申报人的 34,000 美元线，因此运行 IRS 出版物 915 中的工作表，36,000 美元福利中的 16,400 美元算作收入。另外 19,600 美元是免税的。

联邦总收入为 30,000 美元加上 16,400 美元，即 46,400 美元。

现在扣分。 2026 年，单个申报者的标准扣除额为 16,100 美元。 65 岁或以上的任何人均可额外获得 2,050 美元。 2025 年通过的税法在 2028 年之前为 65 岁及以上的人增加了高达 6,000 美元的扣除额，这位退休人员可以全额扣除，因为收入低于 75,000 美元，收入开始减少。这三项加起来为 24,150 美元。

应税收入为 46,400 美元减去 24,150 美元，即 22,250 美元。前 12,400 美元按 10% 征税，即 1,240 美元，其余 9,850 美元按 12% 征税，即 1,182 美元。当年的联邦账单为 2,422 美元，称之为 2,400 美元。这占这位退休人员花费的 66,000 美元的 3.7%，扣除联邦税后每月还剩下大约 5,300 美元。大多数州根本不对社会保障征税。

这位出生于 1958 年的退休人员在 2031 年 73 岁时开始要求提款。这使得 IRA 可以在五年内以低利率一次转入罗斯账户。

填补 12% 的剩余部分每年可转换 15,200 美元。额外的联邦税为 3,400 美元，换算后的实际税率为 22.2%，因为换算后的每一美元也会将更多的社会保障纳入应税栏目，直到 81% 的福利被征税。五年后，将 76,000 美元转移到罗斯，无需提款即可增长，并且免税。即使进行转换，收入仍保持在 109,000 美元以下的 34,480 美元，其中 Medicare 的 B 部分保费每月 202.90 美元开始收取附加费。

假设股票方每年赚取7%，远低于标准普尔500指数过去十年回报率的15.2%，阶梯继续支付4.9%，提款每年增加2.5%。到 73 岁时，阶梯支出已降至约 208,000 美元，基金已增长至约 491,000 美元，IRA 持有约 700,000 美元。

700,000 美元的首次提款要求为 700,000 美元除以 26.5（IRS 除数为 73），即 26,400 美元。到那时，该计划每年已提取 33,900 美元，因此所需金额不会迫使您额外支出。 73岁的工作有所不同：在经济好的一年出售足够的基金，将十年的提款重新投入到阶梯中。

十年测试是押注股票方将有十年的时间工作。根据标普 500 指数基金 2016 年 11 月至今本周的记录，如果将股息再投资，过去 10 年将把 35 万美元变成约 144 万美元。同一记录中最差的十年，即 1999 年底至 2009 年底，如果将股息再投资，则损失约 10%，只剩下 316,000 美元。阶梯可以让你等待，而不卖掉。
